title: Salvation review: Emin Alper examines collective violence
body_md:
Emin Alper's Salvation has been described in a newly published review as a tense, atmospheric examination of the conditions that make collective violence possible. The Turkish filmmaker's fifth feature follows Burning Days, which appeared in the Un Certain Regard section at Cannes in 2022. Rather than treating a shocking act as an isolated dramatic event, his latest film investigates the social relationships and beliefs surrounding it.

## A community under pressure

The story takes place in a mountainous Turkish village where Mesut, played by Caner Cindoruk, lives in the shadow of his younger brother, Sheikh Ferit, portrayed by Feyyaz Duman. Their grandfather once occupied an influential position in the community, but the family inherited that authority through Ferit rather than through the older sibling. The resulting imbalance is one of several tensions that shape their relationship.

Meanwhile, disputes over land and concerns about outsiders contribute to an increasingly distrustful atmosphere. Domestic problems intersect with the village's broader anxieties, allowing the film to examine the relationship between private grievances and public authority without reducing its subject to the misconduct of a single individual.

The reviewer praises Cindoruk's performance, particularly the way his portrayal reflects Mesut's changing standing within the community. The film also considers the responsibilities of the people around him and the consequences of allowing prejudice to influence collective decisions.

## An uncertain boundary between dreams and reality

One of the film's distinguishing formal choices is its treatment of dreams and visions. Alper does not consistently signal when the narrative has moved away from ordinary reality. Viewers must therefore remain attentive to the limitations of the characters' perspectives rather than accepting everything on screen as straightforward evidence.

According to the review, this approach serves a purpose beyond creating suspense. The disorientation complements a broader examination of distrust, competing interpretations and the social consequences of claims that go unchallenged. Religious imagery and local traditions are woven into that atmosphere, encouraging questions about how authority is exercised.

Salvation draws inspiration from a real massacre in Turkey's Mardin province in 2009. The film is not presented simply as a reconstruction of that tragedy. Instead, its fictional narrative provides space to examine collective responsibility, exclusion and the relationship between belief and power.

The review suggests that Salvation may particularly interest audiences drawn to politically engaged cinema and psychological drama. Its assessment is a critical response to the film, not an independently conducted screening review by TapSeen. The source does not specify a general theatrical release date.

[Source review](https://variety.com/2026/film/reviews/salvation-review-1236660920)
